title: Tempura Vegetables
subtitle: light, crisp battered vegetables in Japanese style
excerpt: Tempura is the Japanese technique of coating vegetables in a light, barely-mixed batter and frying them in hot oil until pale and crisp. The key is cold water, minimal mixing, and hot oil. The batter should be lumpy -- that is correct.
sourceNotes: Tempura was introduced to Japan by Portuguese missionaries and traders in the sixteenth century. The name derives from the Latin word Quatuor Anni Tempora (the four seasons). Japanese cooks refined the batter into an exceptionally light, crisp coating, and tempura became a cornerstone of Japanese cuisine.

content.text: Tempura batter is unlike other batters. It is mixed for just a few seconds, left lumpy, and made with ice-cold water. These three things -- cold water, minimal mixing, and hot oil -- are what produce the famously light, crisp coating. Fry in small batches so the oil temperature stays high.

items.prepNote: use ice-cold water for the batter -- do not overmix
use soy sauce -- for the dipping sauce

content.text: Make the batter just before frying: whisk together the flour, beaten egg, and 150ml of ice-cold water. Mix briefly -- lumps are fine. Overmixing develops gluten and makes the batter heavy.
Heat the oil in a large saucepan to 180°C. Test with a drop of batter -- it should sink slightly and float back up within 2 seconds.
Dip each piece of vegetable into the batter, letting the excess drip off. Lower carefully into the oil.
Fry in small batches for 2 to 3 minutes until pale golden and crisp. Do not overcrowd the pan.
Drain on kitchen paper. Season with salt flakes.
Serve immediately with a small bowl of soy sauce for dipping.

items.symptom: Batter is heavy and doughy, not crisp
items.cause: Batter overmixed or water not cold enough
items.fix: Use ice-cold water -- add a few ice cubes to the water before measuring. Mix the batter with chopsticks or a fork for just a few seconds. Lumps are fine and help keep the coating light.

content.text: Tempura is one of Japan's most celebrated dishes. The lightness of the batter is the skill. In Japan, specialist tempura restaurants (tenpura-ya) fry each piece to order and serve it immediately. At home, keeping the batter cold and the oil hot gives the best result.
